images.caption: Figure 1:We introduceThinkWorld, a vision-language-action framework that learns transferable Chain-of-Dynamics (CoD) reasoning from diverse human and robot experiences. CoD captures action-induced dynamics across embodiments and is reinforced through future imagination, enabling robust generalization in the real world and skill composition guided by human videos.

Figure 2:ThinkWorld architecture and training stages.In stage (a), supervised fine-tuning (SFT) tokenizes robot actions and annotated human hand motions into a unified discrete motion space to ground Chain-of-Dynamics (CoD) reasoning, while CoD-conditioned imagination predicts the future visual feature. In stage (b), reinforcement learning (RL) uses the alignment between imagined and observed futures as a scalable reward for CoD reasoning over human and robot videos, strengthening action reasoning without motion annotations and improving guidance for continuous control.

Figure 3:Real-world out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization.Success rates for color matching, cup hanging, and sorting under in-domain and OOD conditions. OOD settings introduce new colors, objects, environments, or sorting trajectories, as illustrated below the plots. ThinkWorld achieves the highest OOD success rates across all three tasks, despite substantial drops for the baselines.

Figure 4:Composing atomic robot skills from a human demonstration.Thetopshows atomic robot skills, while themiddleshows a human demonstration that provides the complete task composition, e.g., open→\rightarrowput-left→\rightarrowclose. Guided by this human demonstration, ThinkWorld composes the corresponding robot skills and executes the complete task in a single rollout at thebottom.

denote datasets. Similar motions cluster across human and robot data

Figure 7:Effect of Chain-of-Dynamics (CoD) on future prediction.We compare future DINO predictions under generated, shuffled, empty, and no-CoD conditions against the current and future ground-truth features. The generated CoD captures the future-state structure, whereas the other variants largely remain similar to the current state and fail to reflect the expected future change.

Figure 8:Attention analysis of CoD.We visualize attention from CoD tokens to the current observation. Across human and robot examples, CoD attends to action-relevant regions, including human hands, robot arms, and manipulated objects, highlighting its focus on motion-relevant cues.

Figure 15:Qualitative future-prediction results.Each row is one episode.
The first two columns show the current and ground-truth future RGB
observations, and the next two show PCA projections of the
ground-truth DINO features for those frames.
The remaining five columns show the predicted future DINO features
under different CoD conditions: with CoD, shuffled CoD, empty CoD,
a CoD taken from a different (donor) episode, and without CoD.
All PCA panels share one color mapping.

Figure 17:Additional attention visualizations.Attention maps from CoD and future-prediction tokens to the input observation. CoD attention concentrates on dynamic, task-relevant regions, while future-prediction attention is more broadly distributed across the scene.

Figure 18:One-second-ahead future predictions during closed-loop SimplerEnv rollouts.For each task, the upper row shows observations actually reached by the policy, while the lower row shows PCA-projected future representations predicted at the preceding replanning horizon. Each column pairs a prediction with the observation at its target time, so their scene structure should correspond. The close qualitative alignment in layout and task progress shows that the predictions track the states encountered during closed-loop execution. The initial frame has no preceding prediction.
